title: Cisco D9036 encoder
description: The D9036 Modular Encoding Platform, via Frikanalen/d9036_exporter. Provisioned by roles/d9036_exporter -- edits made in the UI are overwritten on the next Ansible run.

panels.title: Exporter
panels.description: d9036_up: the exporter reached the encoder and got card inventory, readiness and alarms out of it. Down means the encoder, its management interface or the automation login is unavailable — not that the encoder has stopped encoding.

panels.title: System
panels.description: IsSystemReady. The D9036 reports eSystemStartup_Ready once the controller has finished bringing the chassis up; anything else means it is still starting, and services on it are not yet running.

panels.title: Redundancy role
panels.description: GetDeviceState. Which half of the main/backup pair this chassis currently believes it is. A chassis that has changed role since yesterday did so for a reason.

panels.title: Major alarms
panels.description: Open alarms the encoder classes Critical or Major. These are the ones that mean something on air is wrong or about to be.

panels.title: Minor alarms
panels.description: Open alarms the encoder classes Minor or Warning — worth reading, not worth waking up for.

panels.title: Cards present
panels.description: Cards the chassis enumerates. A drop here is a card that has gone away entirely, which no alarm severity fully conveys.

panels.title: Open alarms by severity
panels.description: Counted from the same MM_GetAllOpenMsgStatus call the table below expands. Steps up are new alarms; steps down are alarms clearing.

panels.title: Open alarms by class
panels.description: Same alarms, cut the other way. Quality is the transport-stream and input-signal side, Processing the encoding pipeline, Equipment the hardware itself — which of the three moves tells you where to look.

panels.title: Active alarms
panels.description: Every open alarm, oldest first. The exporter deliberately does not carry the alarm's human-readable text as a label — it is unbounded cardinality — so look type_id up in the chassis web UI's message log. Board 65534 means the chassis rather than a card; an em dash is a field the alarm does not use.

panels.title: Card inventory
panels.description: gva_card, as the chassis reports it. Slot, board type and the state the controller has it in — the quickest answer to 'is the encoder card actually there and running'.

panels.title: Cards by state
panels.description: How many cards are in each state over time. Flat is healthy; a card moving between states is a card resetting, and this is where a reset that happened while nobody was watching shows up.

panels.title: Pool utilisation
panels.description: Fraction of each hardware pool the configured services have claimed. Aggregated with max rather than sum on purpose: the chassis reports the same pool once per engine class that can draw on it, so summing counts the same silicon several times over.

panels.title: Free units by pool
panels.description: The same pools in absolute units. A step down without anyone touching the configuration means the chassis has taken resources for itself, usually because a card came back up and reclaimed them.

panels.title: Services that would still fit
panels.description: For each service class the chassis can run, how many more instances of it the free pools would carry: the smallest floor(free / per-instance) across every pool that class draws on. Answers 'can we add another HD H.264 encode' without doing the arithmetic by hand. These compete for the same silicon — the answers are alternatives, not a shopping list.

targets.expr: min by (parent_class) (floor(max by (parent_class, resource_class) (d9036_hardware_resource_free{device=~"$device"}) / max by (parent_class, resource_class) (d9036_hardware_resource_quantity{device=~"$device"})))

panels.title: Timekeeping
panels.description: The encoder stamps its output from this clock, and its alarm log from it too. A drifting D9036 makes both harder to reason about.

panels.title: Offset from peer
panels.description: How far the chassis clock is from each peer. 127.127.1.0 is the local undisciplined clock and 169.254.255.255 the broadcast placeholder; neither means anything. The real peer is the one on 192.168.3.0/24.

panels.title: Delay and jitter
panels.description: Round-trip delay and jitter to each peer. Jitter climbing while offset stays put is a network problem rather than a clock problem.

panels.title: NTP peers
panels.description: Peer table as ntpq would print it. Tally eNTP_TC_SysPeer is the peer currently disciplining the clock; reachability is the octal shift register, so 377 is eight good polls out of eight.

panels.title: Collection health
panels.description: The exporter's two data sources, separately: emi_up is the XML inventory interface, iiop_up the web-to-IIOP bridge that carries readiness, alarms and NTP. One down and the other up narrows the fault to one half of the appliance's automation stack.

panels.title: Collection duration
panels.description: How long the encoder took to answer a full collection. The exporter serialises collections, so this climbing towards the scrape interval is the warning that scrapes are about to start queueing behind each other.

panels.title: Device message rate
panels.description: Rate of change of the newest sequence number in the chassis message buffer — how fast the encoder is logging. A quiet box logs almost nothing, so a sustained rise is the chassis complaining about something even when no alarm is open. Negative values are the sequence number wrapping at 32767 and are clamped away.
